name: Omar Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the independent Work Futures Panel. Your answers are confidential; what happens on a normal day building or repairing power lines?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Our electricity company sends a crew sheet before first light, and I check the truck stock while the kettle boils. Once we’re out, I might replace a pole crossarm or help restore a line after wind damage; the crew still has to test and make the site safe.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what has changed in your own routine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving a fault with the crew and watching the houses light up again. I use AI every day to turn my rough job notes into a clean handover, but I check every switch number before it leaves my phone; my partner Nia says I still talk about feeders at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my crew the note app is a decent pencil, not another lineworker. If the job and pay stay much the same, I can spend less time typing and more time checking the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I’m pleased, because I have a mortgage and two school-age children, and we’re comfortable on my higher lineworker pay. We have more than six months set aside, though a long stretch without overtime would still squeeze the fun money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep using my daily AI handover tool and checking the switch numbers against the signed job sheet. In the first year I’d set aside another fifty from each normal pay cheque for the children’s school trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work, with the usual awareness that a storm can eat a weekend. A small gain in paperwork time would be welcome.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the handover tool writes a wrong switch number?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I stop the message and correct the number before the next crew sees it. My apprenticeship taught me the signed sheet, not a tidy sentence, is the thing to trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is the school money different from your existing savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fifty would leave each new pay cheque before we spend it. Our existing reserve stays where it is for the mortgage or a genuine emergency.

say: **AI notes** save me typing time while crews continue building and repairing lines.
I would tell colleagues to check every **switch number** before a handover goes out.
think: Our **mortgage** and children still make a steady wage matter, even with over six months saved.
I see a small **paperwork gain** without a threat to the physical work.
do: **Continue** using my daily handover tool and checking switch numbers against signed sheets.
**Save** fifty from each regular pay cheque for school trips during the first year.
feel: **Calm** about the job, though weekend storm calls still have a cost.
S0.quote: My apprenticeship taught me the signed sheet, not a tidy sentence, is the thing to trust.
fieldNote: Omar already uses **AI daily** for handovers and treats it as a draft tool, not a safety authority.
His new **school-trip saving** comes from future pay and sits apart from the household emergency reserve.

steps.text: Continue checking AI handovers against signed switch sheets
Save fifty from each regular pay cheque for school trips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say our planners may lose some scheduling and buying work before anyone invents a robot I trust on a pole. I’d volunteer to test how the new job tickets reach crews, because I already work with AI notes each day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the best chance of keeping good pay is becoming the person who catches the bad handoff between software and site. The line crew still does physical work, but a cheaper planning office could send us more jobs per shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d show our supervisor the mistakes I have logged in handovers and ask to join the ticket trial next month. During its first year I’d learn the new planning screen, then keep a record of false materials lists so the store team can fix them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy about being rushed, though I don’t expect my line job to vanish soon. The danger is a neat plan that steals the time needed for a safe check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Give me one materials error you would put in the record.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d note a ticket calling for the wrong connector size and photograph the label on the part we actually used. Then the store team can trace why the generated list was off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take extra jobs if the system made the route shorter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the crew can still inspect and isolate each site properly. A shorter drive is useful, but it does not shorten a voltage test.

say: **Planning** and buying may change first, while line crews still handle the physical work.
I would volunteer for a **job-ticket trial** to catch errors reaching the truck.
think: My **pay** looks reasonably secure, but software may push more calls into each shift.
I want to be the person who catches the **handoff error** before a crew loses time or safety.
do: **Join** the company’s job-ticket trial if the supervisor accepts my request.
**Learn** the new planning screen and record wrong materials lists for the store team.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed checks, despite expecting continued linework.
S1.quote: A shorter drive is useful, but it does not shorten a voltage test.
fieldNote: He brings an existing **AI habit** to a proposed company trial, unlike someone trying tools for the first time.
His concern is **pace**: fewer planning staff could leave crews with more work per shift, even while their jobs remain.

steps.text: Join the company job-ticket trial if accepted
Record wrong connector lists for the store team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew full thinking AI by 2028 could run dispatch, but people still have to climb, isolate and repair until capable robots arrive around 2031. I’d ask for a real trial schedule, because nobody should learn robot safety from a sales clip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I could probably learn the new controls quickly, but I do not know how many crew posts survive after 2031. My savings buy time, not another thirty years of mortgage payments and children’s costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the electricity company for access to any supervised robot test and for the training rules before 2028. I’d also set an extra three hundred a month from regular pay into our reserve and check nearby utility openings every quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, and I say that even though I enjoy technology. My daily software habit does not guarantee a place on a smaller line crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the test supervisor to let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want to operate the stop control on a de-energised training pole and see how the machine reports an unexpected fault. I would not ask to try it beside a live line first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nia before you save the extra three hundred?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my partner Nia that the extra saving means fewer weekend trips this year. We would agree on it after looking at the mortgage and both children’s activity fees.

say: **2028 thinking AI** may take dispatch before robots can handle line repairs around 2031.
I would demand a **supervised test** before anyone relies on robot work beside a live line.
think: I can learn **controls**, but that alone will not guarantee a place if crews shrink.
Our strong **reserve** buys time, not years of mortgage and child costs.
do: **Request** a supervised robot test and its training rules before 2028.
**Save** three hundred more each month from regular pay after reviewing family costs.
**Check** nearby utility openings each quarter in the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about future crew size despite enjoying new technology.
S2.quote: My daily software habit does not guarantee a place on a smaller line crew.
fieldNote: He distinguishes enthusiasm for **AI tools** from certainty about a future lineworker post.
His **three-hundred saving** is conditional on a household budget review and comes from new pay.

steps.text: Request supervised robot testing and training rules
Save three hundred monthly from regular pay after budget review
Check nearby utility openings each quarter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say thinking AI in 2031 and capable robots around 2034 give an electricity company time to train a few crews properly. I would put my name down for a real training scheme as soon as one is offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I would like to move from climbing all day into testing equipment and teaching crews, but I cannot assume such a job will exist. My certificate and apprenticeship give me the practical base; I would need instruction on the robot itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d ask our training lead which technical module counts toward any equipment-testing role and enroll if the company funds it. I’d also volunteer for a supervised dead-line trial if offered and keep my present crew shifts while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautiously interested, more than frightened. Five years lets me test whether the new role is real before I gamble with our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the module worth your evenings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want a named qualification and paid time to practise on the actual equipment. A glossy online badge would not justify missing the children’s evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the company funds no course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stay on the crew and ask other nearby utilities about training openings. I would not spend our mortgage reserve on a course with no stated job route.

say: **2031 thinking AI** gives time to prepare before capable line robots around 2034.
I would join a **real training scheme** if the company offers one.
think: An **equipment-testing role** could use my apprenticeship, but an opening is not guaranteed.
I will protect the **mortgage reserve** from courses with no clear job route.
do: **Ask** the training lead about a qualifying technical module this year.
**Enroll** if the company funds the module and offers paid equipment practice.
**Volunteer** for a supervised dead-line robot trial if available.
feel: **Interested** and cautious, with time to verify a role before changing course.
S3.quote: A glossy online badge would not justify missing the children’s evenings.
fieldNote: He sees a **training route** through a funded module and actual equipment practice, not a generic online badge.
He would keep **current shifts** and seek nearby employers if his own company offers nothing.

steps.text: Ask the training lead about a funded equipment module
Enroll in the funded module if paid practice is offered
Volunteer for a supervised robot trial if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that thinking AI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 leave time to build a careful inspection method. A robot could take the hard lift, while someone still checks its joints and the ground it stands on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’ll be in my fifties by then, and I might welcome fewer ladder days. Still, I would rather keep a good lineworker wage than jump to a lower-paid desk job just because a screen looks clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the next year I’d document the tricky faults I encounter and ask the training lead to let me help with one apprentice session. I’d keep using AI for my daily handovers, and revisit any robot course when there is a real company timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m calm about having a decade, provided we use it. I can make a measured move without asking my family to absorb a blind pay cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show an apprentice first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d show how a loose connection looks after a wet week and make them test before touching anything. The tool can list faults, but the apprentice needs to recognise one on a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you invest family savings in a robot business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have no business plan for that and the savings back our mortgage. I would rather seek a paid inspection or training role if it becomes available.

say: **2036 thinking AI** and capable robots around 2039 give line crews a decade to prepare.
I would build a **fault record** that apprentices can use in real inspections.
think: Fewer **ladder days** may suit me in my fifties, if a paid role exists.
I would not put our **mortgage savings** into a robot business without a plan.
do: **Document** tricky line faults during the next year for apprentice teaching.
**Help** with one apprentice session if the training lead agrees.
**Continue** AI handovers while waiting for a real company robot timetable.
feel: **Calm** with a decade to prepare and room to protect family income.
S4.quote: A robot could take the hard lift, while someone still checks its joints and the ground it stands on.
fieldNote: He imagines a **later-career shift** into inspection or teaching but keeps pay and an actual post in view.
His daily **AI use** continues; he does not treat ordinary handovers as new training.

steps.text: Document tricky line faults for apprentice teaching
Help with an apprentice session if invited

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the company could change dispatch fast and then decide how many crews it needs before I have seen a robot work safely. I would need a published test and training timetable, paid practice, and an honest headcount plan for line crews.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the right to press stop when a machine and a tired crew disagree. I can learn a new control in a day, but trust on a wet pole takes longer.

headlineQuote: I can learn a new control in a day, but trust on a wet pole takes longer.
portrait: Omar is a forty-three-year-old **lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a mortgage, two schoolchildren, higher pay and over six months saved.
He uses **AI daily** for handovers, checking every switch number against the signed job sheet.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious** about a smaller future crew despite his willingness to learn controls.
With more time, he would seek **funded training** and paid equipment practice while protecting the family reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remake dispatch before he sees safe robot trials or knows future crew numbers.
whatWouldHelp: A published **test timetable**, paid practice and an honest line-crew headcount plan would help him prepare.
